item.title: Meeting of two lost souls: can Pochettino make it work at Manchester United? | Barney Ronay
item.description: Manager has been hurt by experiences at elite clubs but several players at Old Trafford could fit his playing style Welcome, Mauricio, to the meat grinder. Or rather, welcome back. We’ve been expecting you. There is nothing surprising in the news Manchester United may be on the verge of appointing Mauricio Pochettino. United are always on the verge of appointing Pochettino. This is a club that has spent 13 years hiring and firing the same structurally doomed manager – same shellshocked eyes, same irresolvable macro-problems – and the last eight years almost but not quite doing this to Pochettino. Well, maybe we’re finally here. Maybe he just needed to be broken enough to make it fit. And who knows, perhaps there is even a kind of accidental synergy here. Continue reading...

item.title: Psychology says constant scrolling before work may be a form of avoidance
item.description: Procrastination often stems from evading unpleasant emotions tied to challenging tasks. Techniques like dividing tasks into manageable parts and scheduling specific times for leisure can effectively combat procrastination.

item.title: Tens of thousands attend Polish nationalist march days after shootings
item.description: Tens of thousands of Polish nationalist sympathisers gathered in Warsaw Wednesday for an annual Independence Day March, just days after a deadly shooting spree in Krakow that shook the country. The event is held each November 11 to commemorate the ending in 1918 of 123 years of partition by Russia, Prussia and Austria. The event is a magnet for all shades of Poland's right wing -- from conservative-nationalists aligned with its Law and Justice (PiS) party to far-right and radical groups. FRANCE 24's Carys Garland reports.

item.title: Thomas Tuchel keeps laser focus on ‘unfinished business’ with England

It will not matter whether there is an approach from a big club before the next tournament. United can pay about £7m to get Pochettino out of his deal, but the Football Association does not have to worry about being forced to let Tuchel go. “There’s no intention [of leaving],” Tuchel said. “I signed the contract. He declared that he was “absolutely” willing to accept the results, would look forward to working with Democrats and that deportation policies might have been “ too tough ”. item.title: Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends? | Adrian Chiles
item.description: After Peta’s call ‘to reject mischaracterisations of chickens’, I wonder what they would make of Polish representations of polecats and Croatian cuckoos Chickens don’t have it easy. On top of living largely crap, short lives, they endure the ignominy of collectively being a byword for cowardice. The campaign group People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) has written to the Oxford English Dictionary asking for this definition of “chicken” to be changed. Naturally enough, there are those who have been unafraid to holler “Woke nonsense!” as loud as cocks crowing. For my part, I think Peta is right to stick up for chickens, but I’m not sure removing a definition – assuming definition-removal is a thing – would make any difference. Chicken, in this sense, is in common use as an adjective, a verb and a noun. It’s got deep roots that are going to take some shifting. And any such move could open up a right can of worms (sorry, worms). What about the vulture, rat, shark and sloth lobb

item.title: Stacy Keach obituary
item.description: Versatile American stage and screen actor whose roles ranged from Hamlet to the tough private eye Mike Hammer There have been few actors as inexhaustible as Stacy Keach, who has died aged 85. Throughout a long career that began in his childhood he was equally active in theatre, films and TV, moving from the sublime to the ridiculous and back again with aplomb. Perhaps it was his ubiquity and eclecticism that caused him to be so underrated. Keach meant different things to different people. To theatregoers, he was a fine Shakespearean actor, acclaimed for his Hamlet, who was also adept in other classics and musicals (Barnum, Camelot, The King and I). To the filmgoer, he was one of the faces of Hollywood in the 1970s. To the television viewer, Keach was the tough private eye Mike Hammer, in the 80s TV series and spinoffs based on the novels by Mickey Spillane. Continue reading...

As Jones later confided: “This Welsh bloke came up to me and said: ‘You almost look human with your glasses on.’” Next up is a reunion with a few former friends – and foes – at Twickenham. item.title: ‘Young, Black and female in Brixton is hard’: ​from football to Top Boy and wordplay, the inspiring journey of UK rapper Cristale
item.description: Crystal Palace FC or Oxbridge beckoned, but the multitalented MC kept forging her way towards music. She explains how she poured every aspect of herself into her debut mixtape Two weeks before we meet, UK rapper Cristale was scrambling down a cliff face to a secluded black pebbled beach in Dover, racing an incoming tide with fewer than 90 minutes to shoot the video for her single I’m Okay With Being Lonely. She’d never hiked before in her life. “I was wearing head-to-toe Stone Island, no hiking gear, full face of makeup, edges laid and Mum was doing my touch-ups on a rusty ladder,” she laughs. item.title: The space rocket I could have been aboard explodes: Rhiannon Adam’s best photograph
item.description: ‘I was chosen to go around the Moon on a SpaceX starship. Preparations took over my life. Then, four minutes into watching a rocket on a test flight, it broke apart. And that was the end of my adventure’ This photograph was taken on 20 April 2023 from the VIP section of SpaceX’s launch viewing area, looking out from South Padre Island, Texas, towards Boca Chica, a nature reserve near the Mexican border which is home to SpaceX’s Starbase launchpad. In 2021, I and seven other civilians were selected from an open call to go around the Moon on a free SpaceX Starship flight funded by the Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa. For me, the story also became about being plucked from obscurity and planted in this very surreal world I could never have imagined being a part of in a million years. item.description: Far-right populists remain insurgent and pro-EU governments are braced for Trump’s betrayal. But the midterms also showed that democracy can fight back • Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here “Is Maga dead?” asked Margaret, a Guardian reader in Switzerland, in a live Q&A with our correspondents after the seismic US midterm elections. He asks legendary showrunners about their experience ‘Write, write, write until your fingers break!” That was Chekhov’s advice to writers. Until I started writing for television I thought I understood what he meant. I thought I knew what writing was: the solitude, the making yourself do it, the finger-shattering pain of doing it seriously, on your own. As well as being chief film critic for the Guardian, I have written fiction and in some ways the basic technical challenge has not been so very different from cinema criticism; after having had the idea, or having seen the film, you have to go away on your own and turn the computer on. item.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
item.description: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. item.title: Bone broth, sweets ban and acupuncture: Harry Kane’s road to record England cap
item.description: Obsessive attention to detail is helping striker to reach new heights – and a 126th international appearance on Thursday It was Harry Kane’s dirty little secret. Something the England captain got up to after matches. He felt he deserved the indulgence. Yes, it can be revealed, Kane loved to reward himself after a gruelling 90 minutes with a bag of sweets. “I do like a Haribo,” he said with a smile after the Nations League win against Czechia in Prague at the end of September. No more. At the beginning of last season, Kane took the decision to cut out the naughty treats. After a while, he noticed a difference. He felt sharper; able to sprint more, make a greater number of accelerations. Was it down to this latest entry on the list of personal sacrifices? Or was it a consequence of his broader health regime, the scope of which is mind-blowing? Continue reading...

item.title: Chicken curry and potato croquettes: Ranie Saidi’s recipes for a Malaysian feast
item.description: Leeks play a major part in two Malaysian-inspired dishes: they melt into coconut in a marvellous chicken curry, and pair perfectly with peas in crunchy potato croquettes Since moving from Malaysia to London more than a decade ago, I’ve slowly brought leeks into my everyday cooking. Their gentle sweetness reminds me of banana shallots, and I love how they melt into this chicken gulai . Bergedil ( or begedil or perkedel) have always been one of my favourite street-food snacks, and are found at stalls across Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia. In Malay cooking, they’re often made using mashed potato that’s mixed with minced meat, shaped and fried, but my version uses leeks, frozen peas and leftover herbs, plus an orange, chilli and yoghurt dip. item.title: ‘Homosexuality was coined by a Hungarian’: the gay-sauna travelogue questioning central Europe’s illiberal image
item.description: A new book, With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna, reveals the deep-rooted queer subcultures in cities from Budapest to Prague – defying regional stereotypes and inspiring an art exhibition on masculinity The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein argued that our understanding of reality is fundamentally bound by and shaped by the language we use to talk about it. But there is one place where the Vienna-born thinker’s argument ceases to make sense. “Gay saunas are spaces where language dies,” says Vratislav Maňák, a Czech writer and literary scholar. With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna, a book that made a major splash when it was published in Czech and German earlier this year, Maňák fictionalises Wittgenstein, who had romantic relations with both men and women , entering a Viennese Herrensauna called Kaiserbründl, hailed in newspapers at the time as “the most stylish bathing establishment in the world”. Continue reading...

item.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season three review – this dull show’s revamp is too little, too late
item.description: They’ve sidelined the harfoots, introduced a Stranger Things star and thrown in full-blooded romance. It’s probably not enough to stop the fantasy prequel feeling boring, though It might seem strange to characterise the leading streaming show from one of the most dominant corporations on the planet as a scrappy underdog. But after a lavish-but-dramatically stilted debut in 2022 and a similarly well-heeled but darker second season in 2024 , it does feel like prequel series The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is somehow stuck on the back foot. For all its finely wrought art direction and respect for JRR Tolkien’s elaborate high-fantasy taxonomy, this no-expense-spared expansion of the mythos – set in the Second Age of Middle-earth, thousands of years before Bilbo Baggins first went walkabout – is in danger of going down in our own historical annals as simply a bit dull. Never mind more rings, it desperately needs some rizz. Continue reading...

item.title: The thermostat wars tearing couples apart: ‘It’s hard to feel sexy when you’re freezing cold’
item.description: Almost two-thirds of bedfellows disagree about the perfect room temperature – and the issue can affect office workers and housemates too. It oftens lead to subterfuge and skulduggery. So is there any way to reach a truce? Recently I read an item on Threads that made me laugh out loud. “New dating app idea: post your thermostat settings to find your match.” The poster then revealed their own preferences: a balmy 24C by day and a chilly 19C at bedtime. The suggestion elicited a rush of responses. “As someone who married outside their thermostat bracket, all I can say is that this is the most brilliant idea ever,” enthused one user. “Get outta here with that daytime terrarium,” responded another. “Are you storing pallets of produce in your house that you need to keep cold?” chimed in a third. item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03671-2 Analysis reveals these plants face severe habitat loss across the Americas — plus, researchers test a new way to diagnose obesity.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03591-1 A study reports that about 107,000 species are traded worldwide, legally or illegally — more than double a previous estimate.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03660-5 Mapping the movements of wildlife across the Amazon and other regions to their exposure to human activities can inform protection initiatives.

item.title: Salty grains in Saturn’s outermost ring formed from the slow freeze of plumes from the moon Enceladus
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03489-y One of Saturn’s rings consists of a diverse population of icy and rocky grains, each with a distinct composition. How this came about might now have an explanation.

item.title: Cacti are severely threatened by drought in a warming world
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03496-z Forecasts of the effects that climate change will have on biodiversity typically rely on long-term climate averages while excluding extreme events. Projections that include severe drought predict that a majority of the 993 cactus species assessed will see large losses of suitable climatic area: more than 25% of species could lose at least 80% of it by 2100.

item.title: Extraordinary materials shaped by the principles of complex networks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03272-z Network science has inspired the design of materials that spread out their deformation when a force is applied, have tunable stiffness and can control vibrational waves.

item.title: DeepMind's ultra-powerful AI for genome mapping wows scientists
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03673-0 AlphaGenome 2 can predict the types of cells where a DNA variant is likely to act.

item.title: Proteins that form the nuclear pore barrier move like liquids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03428-x Nuclear pores control molecular traffic into and out of the cell nucleus. Measurements in living cells, together with molecular-dynamics simulations, show that flexible protein chains that form the selectivity barriers of nuclear pores are highly mobile, and that a sugar modification and the carrier protein importin-β help to preserve this dynamic state.

item.title: How to avoid aliens and live
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03515-z Silence is golden.

item.title: Earth’s early history told by 3.9-billion-year-old rocks from northern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03499-w Ancient rocks in northern China reveal that by 3.95 billion years ago, surface-altered oceanic crust had been buried rapidly to depths greater than 50 kilometres and partly melted. This crust was derived from a mantle reservoir that had been left behind when the crust separated from the early mantle as early as 4.3 billion years ago.

item.title: Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03621-y Agricultural biotechnology once found itself in opposition to environmental science. Now it could reduce the impact of food systems on global warming and biodiversity loss.

item.title: How I balance my life as a professional surfer and a university researcher
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03183-z Cliff Kapono shares his advice on ways to navigate and grow two different careers.

item.title: Hideki Shirakawa obituary: chemist who showed that plastics can conduct electricity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03633-8 Nobel prizewinner’s accidental discovery led to new forms of materials, light-emitting diodes and solar cells.

item.title: Give biologists the space to be curious, not just better tools
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03669-w Technology is making biological studies more powerful than ever. But people are the real force behind discovery.

item.title: Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03640-9 A promising biotechnology company developed a new approach that might treat a rare disease — but its sole employee didn’t do all the work.

item.title: Move over BMI: new obesity definition is better for predicting your health
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03636-5 A fresh approach considers waist circumference, rather than just weight and height, providing a more accurate classification.

item.title: New culprit in early Alzheimer’s: Blood–brain barrier blocks protective proteins
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03655-2 The brain relies on crucial proteins to maintain neurons. This system is disrupted in mice with neurological disease.

item.title: AI’s energy paradox: will the AI boom strain energy systems or be the source of solutions?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03412-5 Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes is leading a community of interdisciplinary specialists exploring how to make the energy use of artificial intelligence net-positive.

item.title: Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03624-9 Decades-old papers are increasingly being pulled from the literature, bringing a host of challenges.

item.title: Author or just ‘acknowledged’? How women are not gaining full credit for research
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03448-7 An analysis of who is more likely to get authorship than acknowledgement highlights the influence of a researcher’s gender and status.

item.title: Engineered bacteria are weaning farms away from synthetic fertilizers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03641-8 Scientists are editing microbes to supply more nitrogen to staple crops.

item.title: Proposed approach for diagnosing obesity outperforms old method
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03425-0 A framework for diagnosing obesity that was proposed in 2025 incorporates waist circumference and related measures and distinguishes clinical from preclinical obesity on the basis of obesity-induced organ dysfunction. In an international multi-cohort study of 844,108 adults, this framework outperformed conventional body-mass-index-based criteria in diagnosing obesity and stratifying mortality risk.

item.title: Personal incentives for public officials drove a drop in China’s fertility
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03274-x Once the promotion prospects of bureaucrats became tied to birth targets, the country’s one-child policy became more effective. Can the state now reverse this effect?

item.title: Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03409-0 As global energy markets grapple with a period of sustained political volatility, researchers are digging deep for solutions.

item.title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11204-0 Structural and biochemical studies show that the CMG helicase directly recruits PRIMPOL for leading-strand repriming, enabling replication fork restart and limiting post-replicative DNA gaps.

item.title: Bureaucratic incentives shaped effectiveness of the one-child policy in China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11232-w Stronger bureaucratic incentives under China’s one vote veto policy intensified enforcement of the one-child policy, accounting for nearly half of China’s fertility decline during the 1990s.

item.title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5 A large-scale data analysis assesses the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic framework for obesity, finding that this framework, in which BMI is combined with other criteria, such as waist circumference and organ function, is more useful than classifications based on BMI alone.

item.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11256-2 TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact and suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication; a therapeutic strategy is found that corrects UNC13A cryptic splicing by using splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides.

item.title: NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11324-7 The stiffness of the extracellular matrix is identified as a pivotal factor that influences activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro and in vivo.

item.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11282-0 An electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions enables reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes, and is validated in metal–iodine batteries.

item.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11308-7 IL-1β from neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby brown adipocytes in a low-UCP1 state; cold temperature reduces IL-1β via sympathetic nerves, leading to transition to a high-UCP1 state and increased thermogenesis, while higher temperatures have the opposite effect.

item.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11230-y Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.

item.title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11259-z The rice RNA-binding protein NIB1 detects 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide products from insect saliva RNase, forming nuclear condensates that recruit EDS1 to activate defence, revealing a conserved messenger-based immune pathway in plants.

item.title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11278-w Flexible tidal turbine blades with passive trailing-edge deformation match the energy yield of active pitch-controlled blades while reducing fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third, lowering maintenance complexity.

item.title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11280-2 Analysis of a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, China, reveals a composition suggesting a low-temperature altered basaltic source, that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean, was most likely transported to mantle depths through a transient subduction event and partially melted to produce the trondhjemite.

item.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x Microplastic burdens in Brazilian tapirs and anteaters rise with human-modified land use and proximity to development, however animals in remote habitats also carry microplastics, showing that landscape change and individual space use jointly shape wildlife exposure.

item.title: Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11240-w A distinct physical nuclear state acquired by embryos at the beginning of life supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

item.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11264-2 Experiments in mouse models show that immunoglobulin A in the gut lumen has a role in regulating the turnover of colon epithelial cells and reduces the susceptibility of mice to colorectal cancer.

item.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11269-x The somatic evolutionary histories of haematopoietic cells in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis show that the clonal dynamics of blood comply with a set of simple evolutionary rules.

item.title: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11191-2 A network-science-based framework that embeds network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials is used to produce scale-rich metamaterials that exhibit properties inaccessible to traditional single-scale systems.

item.title: The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11276-y PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS, facilitating primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis.

item.title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11262-4 A novel therapeutic modality enforces non-native androgen receptor (AR)–p300/CBP interactions to collapse AR transcriptional programs, producing super-inhibitory, lineage-selective suppression of metastatic prostate cancer and establishing domain-alteration chimeras as a broadly applicable therapeutic strategy leveraging induced proximity.

item.title: Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11258-0 Nuclear pore proteins maintain a fluid, spatially organized barrier through coordinated molecular interactions, explaining how cells achieve selective transport and reconciling competing models of pore structure.

item.title: Severe drought and warming increase the extinction risk of cacti
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11265-1 Severe drought and warming will substantially increase the loss of suitable climatic area for cactus species.

item.title: Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11272-2 A transferable single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric enables high-quality interfaces with two-dimensional semiconductors, yielding near-ideal switching, low hysteresis and ultra-low-power complementary transistors and inverters.

item.title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11241-9 An imaging algorithm using closure-invariant formalism and diffusion-based reconstruction applied to supermassive black hole very long baseline radio interferometry datasets enables independent recovery of the ring-like shadow and mass that is free from the usual calibration and imaging assumptions.

item.title: Mitochondrial protein import defects enhance tumour immunogenicity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11249-1 Inhibition of mitochondrial protein import can enhance tumour immunogenicity by promoting mitochondrial DNA release.

item.title: Metasurface waveguides for all-day augmented reality glasses
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11277-x An all-day-wearable augmented reality glasses prototype using a dual-layer metasurface-based waveguide and three matched grating patterns achieves a 30° field of view in an 8 × 8-mm2 two-dimensional eyebox while maintaining high luminance efficiency.

item.title: Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images
item.description: A breakthrough in telescope imaging could reveal countless alien worlds that have been hiding in plain sight. Scientists developed a new technique that uses a digital twin of the James Webb Space Telescope to remove the overwhelming glare of stars, making faint exoplanets two to 15 times easier to detect than with conventional methods. The technology has already uncovered a previously hidden planet in existing telescope data and could reveal many more.

item.title: What happens to your brain when the days get darker? - video

Liverpool and Manchester United have reasons to celebrate their No 7. Ajax retired No 14 for Johan Cruyff, Milan their No 3 and No 6 for Paolo Maldini and Franco Baresi respectively and Birmingham their 22 for Jude Bellingham as gestures of respect for their abilities. Other numbers have been retired to mark premature deaths: the No 20 at Liverpool for Diogo Jota, the No 23 at Manchester City for Marc-Vivian Foé, the 21 at Espanyol for Daniel Jarque. item.title: Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth
item.description: A century-old theory about the origins of life on Earth may be wrong. The findings point toward asteroids or chemical processes on Earth as more plausible sources of life's building blocks.

A band will often bring together a very disparate set of people, their only thing in common the fact they’re in the same group. And a good band takes account of the interests and strengths of its members – that’s how you get a unique sound. Being part of this year’s Booker prize judging panel – chaired by Mary Beard, and featuring the writers Patricia Lockwood, Raymond Antrobus and Rebecca Liu – felt much the same. We were all very different, but we had a common cause: to pick a good winner. item.title: Killing the Pope review – the truth behind the attempted murder of John Paul II
item.description: Was the failed assassination of the Polish pope a Soviet plot or simply the work of a deranged hitman? On the afternoon of Wednesday 13 May 1981, St Peter’s Square in Rome was packed with more than 10,000 pilgrims, excited to see the charismatic John Paul II, formerly Karol Wojtyla, archbishop of Kraków. Two and a half years earlier he had become the youngest cardinal to be elected pope in more than a century and the first non-Italian for 455 years. At 5.17pm a man pulled out a concealed pistol and raised it with both hands above the heads of the crowd. He took aim at the pope, only a few metres away, and fired several shots. Then, as he backed away from the shocked bystanders, he tripped and fell, where he lay pinned to the ground by a Franciscan nun until handcuffed by uniformed police. Meanwhile the pope had been hit by two bullets, one in the arm and the other in the abdomen. He was losing blood rapidly. He was rushed to hospital and underwent an operation, before beginning a slow

item.title: Football Daily | Manchester United, Aston Villa and the unseriousness of a 4-4 draw
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Precisely 13,266 games have been played since the inception of the Premier League, and 19 of those matches have finished 4-4 (0.1%), a rarity in a division dominated by the mighty 1-0 (17.6%). It was about time we got one, though. The months of August and September, when teams are still fighting to define their top-flight seasons and fitness and motivation tend to be at their peak, have never seen a single 4-4 draw. As motivation decreases the chances of stupid scorelines increase, and that’s where the 4-4 creeps in. There’s a certain on-the-beachness inherent in the score, and it is no coincidence that it has occurred more in the second half of April, as thoughts drift to the close season and the ineffable pointlessness of a lot of late-campaign football becomes unavoidable, than in the entirety of any other month. After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. item.title: U2: Carnaval de Luz review – rousing, restorative rock from a band ready to take on the world again
item.description: (Island) On their first album of new songs in nearly a decade, even earnest Bono-isms carry weight amid music that is impassioned and rejuvenated Even artists who enjoy a seemingly unstoppable imperial period eventually seem to encounter spells of turbulence when the creative planets no longer align – which has been the story of U2’s last 20 years. Try as they might, nothing has matched their earlier albums – especially that mostly uninterrupted golden run from their 1980 debut Boy to 90s benchmarks Achtung Baby and Zooropa. They’ve tried going more pop, becoming more experimental, touring 1987 colossus The Joshua Tree again and even reworking old songs for 2023’s Songs of Surrender, but nothing has uncorked the genie again, or given the band the kind of relevance they had for so many years. Often, it felt as though they were trying too hard. Continue reading...

item.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
item.description: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

item.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
item.description: Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. Jonathan Wilson Match report: Nottingham Forest 3

item.title: Beethoven: Symphony No 3 album review – thrilling, but Minasi’s determination to shock often feels self-conscious
item.description: Ensemble Resonanz/Minasi (Harmonia Mundi) Riccardo Minasi radically reassesses the Eroica, bringing its acerbic innovation to the fore in a startling and compelling new recording that will surely prompt heated debate In 1816, a young Franz Schubert took a swipe at Beethoven, accusing him of promoting a musical eccentricity that muddled “the agreeable with the repulsive, heroism with howlings and the holiest with harlequinades” in order to “goad people to madness”. In this colours-to-the-mast recording, Riccardo Minasi demonstrates precisely what contemporaries were afraid of with a radical reassessment of the Eroica Symphony. Looking to original sources, he strips away the modifications of centuries to lay the symphony before us in all its acerbic 19th-century innovation. The results are certainly startling. item.title: Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive

Unlike fossil fuel emissions, however, the CO2 we exhale is part of the natural carbon cycle, and scientists say measuring it more accurately could improve climate models.

item.title: ‘Minimal look, maximal politics’: why the black T-shirt signals modern power

A hidden layer rather than the main event. But modern politics has pushed it to the frontlines as a sartorial shortcut to signal power. The progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who this week became the first Muslim elected to the US Senate in history, made a tight black T-shirt his signature look throughout his year-long campaign. item.title: Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined

They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. item.title: An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that an anti-aging drug could help protect people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's disease. Researchers found that just four weeks of low-dose rapamycin improved brain blood flow in healthy middle-aged adults carrying the high-risk APOE4 gene variant, with women showing the strongest benefits. Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss begins.

Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.” To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
